PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Elections Administration. County elections officials administer most elections in California. As part of this work, they print and mail ballots and other voting materials to registered voters. Some state agencies also have workload related to voting. For example, the Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide .
United States Citizenship Required to Vote in Federal, State, and Almost All Local Elections A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in any state or federal election. A noncitizen who votes in a state or federal election can be fined and/or sentenced to prison. A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in the vast majority of local elections. (San Francisco and Oakland have a special process for people who are not U.S. citizens to vote only in school board elections if they are the parent, guardian, or legally recognized caregiver of a student in the school district.)
Voter Registration. In order to vote, people first must register with elections officials. People register to vote in the county where they live. To be eligible to register, a person must be a U.S. citizen, live in California, be at least 18 years old, not currently be in prison, and not be found unable to vote by a court. A person who makes a false statement when attempting to register to vote in California, such as by falsely stating that they are a U.S. citizen, is guilty of the crime of perjury. People can register online through the Secretary of State’s website, by mail, in person at a county elections office, or through the California Department of Motor Vehicles. A voter’s identity is established through the registration process by using their driver’s license number, state identification number, or last four digits of their Social Security number. Voters who do not provide this identifying information through the registration process may be asked to present identification the first time they vote.
Voter Rolls Maintenance. A voter roll is a list of people who are registered to vote. Elections officials are required to keep the voter rolls up to date by removing people who are no longer eligible to vote from the list. For example, elections officials receive regular updates from other government entities to identify people who have died or are in prison.
Voting. All registered voters in California receive a vote by mail (VBM) ballot. Voters can mail their ballot, drop it off at a ballot drop-off location, or vote in person at a voting location. In the November 2024 Presidential Election, about 16 million people voted in California. About 13 million voted using a VBM ballot, and about 3 million voted in person.
Voter Identification. Voters identify themselves when they vote in California. If they vote in person, they typically identify themselves by signing a list of registered voters before voting. If they vote by mail, they identify themselves by signing the envelope of their ballot. Elections officials verify signatures for VBM ballots before counting them. Elections officials generally do not verify signatures from in-person voters before counting the ballots.
California State Auditor’s Office (State Auditor). The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments use money and run their programs. These reviews include performance audits to see if the government is following the law and working efficiently. The State Auditor may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly, while others are done only once.
PROPOSAL
Requires State and Local Elections Officials to Verify U.S. Citizenship Status of Registered Voters. Proposition 39 requires state and local elections officials to make “best efforts” using government data to verify that voters on the rolls are U.S. citizens. Proposition 39 requires elections officials to report every year the percentage of registered voters in each county whose citizenship status has been verified.
Requires Voters to Select Government- Issued Identification for Voting by Mail. Proposition 39 requires new and existing voters to select a government-issued identification in their voter registration to vote by mail.
Requires Voters to Provide Additional Identifying Information to Vote. Proposition 39 requires voters to provide additional identifying information each time they cast a ballot in any election in California. Elections officials would be required to verify voters’ identities before counting their ballots. The identification requirement would depend on whether a voter casts their ballot in person or by mail:
In-Person Voting. When voting in person, Proposition 39 requires voters to present government-issued identification for identity verification.
Voting by Mail. When voting by mail, Proposition 39 requires voters to provide the last four digits of their selected government-issued identification number on the ballot envelope. Elections officials would verify that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information.
Creates New State-Issued Voter Identification Card. Proposition 39 requires the state to provide a voter identification card at no cost to voters who request one. The voter identification card could be used as the government-issued identification that verifies a voter’s identity when voting.
Requires State Auditor to Audit State and County Election Compliance Regularly. In every odd-numbered year, Proposition 39 requires the State Auditor to report how well the state and each county comply with the measure and make recommendations for improvement.
Requires Legislative Action for Full Implementation. Proposition 39 requires the Legislature to pass additional laws to implement the measure. The Legislature would need to clarify several details that are not defined in the proposition, like which forms of identification could be used and what steps would be considered best efforts to verify the citizenship status of registered voters.
FISCAL EFFECTS
State and Local Costs Depend on Future Decisions. Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs each year by tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars . These costs represent less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) The exact cost would depend on future choices made by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters. For example, the costs could vary depending on decisions around the design and requirements of the voter identification card and the number of cards requested. There also could be some amount of savings. These savings would be due to fewer people registered to vote—for example, due to the removal of ineligible voters or eligible voters lacking government-issued identification. These savings likely would not exceed the costs of the measure.
Visit sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/cal-access-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/cal-access-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals) for a list of committees primarily formed to support or oppose this measure.

PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 39
VOTER ID: A BIPARTISAN WAY TO INCREASE TRUST IN OUR ELECTIONS
Democratic, Independent, and Republican voters all agree on one thing: Voter ID is a common-sense reform to increase trust and participation in our elections. That’s why almost half the signatures to put Prop. 39 on the ballot came from Democratic and Independent voters and polls show widespread super-majority support across all political parties for Voter ID.
PROP. 39 KEEPS VOTING ACCESSIBLE AND GUARANTEES A FREE VOTER ID
Prop. 39 keeps mail ballots, extended polling hours and all other conveniences in place for voting accessibility.
Voters can use a variety of easily-obtained government IDs to vote—and this measure even guarantees every voter a FREE Voter ID if they want one.
California currently uses a slow process to check signatures on mail ballots that not only delays election results but also puts your vote at risk of not being counted if your signature is flagged as not matching. Many voters say they cannot always remember how they signed their name years ago when they first registered to vote. In the last election, more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches—and more than 200,000 voters endured hassles just to get their vote to count.
VOTER ID INCREASES PARTICIPATION
Voter ID does not suppress voting—in fact it increases voter participation. Every state with Voter ID laws and free identification for eligible voters that cannot afford or access identification, has seen an increase in voting. Suppression and lower turnout happen when voters do not have trust and confidence in the integrity of the process. Voter ID gives all voters a reason to trust that their vote will matter.
PROP. 39 INCLUDES AUDITS AND CITIZENSHIP VERIFICATION
Prop. 39 holds election officials accountable for keeping California’s voter lists accurate and updated. Election officials will also be required to check voter rolls to ensure only citizens are registered. Prop. 39 requires an independent audit be conducted every two years to give the public the confidence they deserve in the way our elections are conducted.
YES ON PROP. 39: FOR A NON-PARTISAN SOLUTION TO VOTER ID
Politicians and partisan organizations who oppose Prop. 39 are desperately trying to inject toxic partisanship into this debate. That’s because they benefit from unfounded election conspiracy theories and rapidly declining trust in our elections.
In contrast, supporters of Prop. 39 include solid majorities of Democratic, Republican and Independent voters and a diverse coalition including Latino American Political Association, California Women’s Leadership Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the Transparency Foundation, and trusted voting rights organizations. Vote YES on Prop. 39 to create a national model for implementing Voter ID in a bipartisan way.
Margit Whitlock , Democratic Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID
Tafa Jefferson , Republican Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID
Joe Green , Independent Coalition Chair
Californians for Voter ID
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 39
NO on PROP. 39—Stop Trump from rigging our elections. Don’t believe the lies. Prop. 39 MAKES VOTING HARDER, MORE EXPENSIVE, AND LESS SAFE for Californians.

PROP
39
PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
OFFICIAL TITLE AND SUMMARY
PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
Prohibits voting by mail unless voter designates a government-issued identification number for their voter registration.
Invalidates mail ballots if envelope does not include last four digits of a government-issued identification number matching the number designated in the voter’s registration (e.g., if voter designates Social Security number for registration, but provides driver’s license number on envelope, their ballot would not count).
Prohibits voting in person without presenting government-issued identification.
Requires elections officials to annually report percentage of each county’s voters whose citizenship status they have verified.
SUMMARY OF LEGISLATIVE ANALYST'S ESTIMATE OF NET STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT FISCAL IMPACT:
State and local government costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. Costs depend on future decisions by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 39 brings the national debate (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-04-02/democracy-at-risk-california-needs-new-voting-protections-poll-shows) around U.S. election integrity home to California by proposing stricter new voter ID requirements for state elections — mandating that voters present government identification every time they vote in person, or cite a specific government ID number when voting by mail.
The measure is backed by prominent California Republicans and ultrawealthy supporters of President Trump, who is pushing even more onerous voter ID measures at the national level (https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2026-08-23/will-trump-interfere-in-midterms-democrats-their-allies-are-preparing). The measure’s backers say it is necessary to prevent voter fraud and block noncitizens from casting ballots. They contend, without evidence, that such problems are widespread in California.
The measure is opposed by the state’s Democratic establishment and prominent civil rights groups, who say it will disenfranchise many eligible voters, particularly those of color, who are poor or live in rural communities, or who move often or have changed their names. They say the latter group would include many married women.
Advertisement
The opponents also contend — as do many independent election experts — that California already has robust measures for verifying the eligibility and identity of voters, and that voter fraud, including by noncitizens, is exceedingly rare.
A poll by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and co-sponsored by The Times (https://igs.berkeley.edu/research/berkeley-igs-poll) last year found that most Californians support (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-05-09/la-times-igs-poll-on-elections-and-voter-id) the idea of requiring a government ID every time a voter casts a ballot. A more recent Berkeley IGS poll (https://escholarship.org/content/qt2d964377/qt2d964377.pdf) found that when voters were given the added context that supporters say the measure is necessary to prevent fraud and opponents say it could disenfranchise eligible voters, they were much more split (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-04-24/assemblymember-carl-demaios-ballot-measure-will-be-considered-by-voters-in-november).

What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 39 would require anyone voting in person in California to present a government-issued ID, and those voting by mail ballot to include the last four digits of the government-issued ID number they provided when they registered to vote.
In-person voters without ID would be turned away, while mail ballots without an attached ID number that matches their registration would be rejected. Critics note the measure does not explicitly require election officials to reach out to voters to correct or “cure” a ballot that is missing an ID number before rejecting it, as they are required to do when a voter’s ballot signature does not match what’s on file.
The measure also would require the state to provide free voter ID cards to eligible voters upon request, and state and county election officials to verify the U.S. citizenship of registered voters using government data and publicly report the findings of that work.
Advertisement
Under current law, Californians are required to provide identification when registering to vote and must swear under penalty of perjury — a felony — that they are eligible to vote and a U.S. citizen. They must sign their mail ballots, and their signature is compared to the one the state has on file to verify their identity. It is already against the law for noncitizens to vote.
Proposition 39’s provisions echo but are less onerous than those proposed in the SAVE America Act (https://www.latimes.com/world-nation/story/2026-03-14/republican-bill-poses-burden-for-many-u-s-voters), the strict voter ID and proof of citizenship measure Trump is pushing in Congress.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated Proposition 39 would “increase state and local government costs each year by tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars.”

New Analysis: Prop. 39 Would Create New Barriers to Voting for Millions of California Voters
Report Examines How Proposed Requirements Could Make Voting More Difficult, Increase Costs, and Limit Californians’ Say in Policymaking
September 10, 2026 | By Kyra Moeller (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kyra-moeller/)
SACRAMENTO, CA — A new publication (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-39-explained-what-voter-id-would-mean-for-california/) from the California Budget & Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/) (Budget Center) examines Proposition 39, a measure on the November ballot that would establish new voter identification and citizenship verification requirements in California and impose additional responsibilities and costs on state and local election officials.
The analysis finds that Prop. 39 would create unnecessary barriers for millions of eligible California voters, including people who lack an up-to-date driver’s license or other qualifying identification. The measure would also require voters who cast ballots by mail to write the last four digits of a unique identifying number from a government-issued ID on the outside of their ballot envelope, potentially increasing the risk of identity theft. In addition, Prop. 39 would require election officials to use “best efforts” to verify the citizenship status of registered voters using government data — a process the report finds could incorrectly flag eligible US citizens and potentially result in voters being removed from the rolls.
“Prop. 39 would impose new and costly requirements on California voters and election officials without actually addressing a real problem,” said Scott Graves, budget director at the California Budget & Policy Center. “California already has in place strong safeguards to verify voter identity and protect the integrity of elections. Adding new requirements would make it harder for eligible Californians to vote while creating new costs for the state.”
The report places Prop. 39 in the broader context of efforts to restrict voting rights and considers what is at stake when barriers to voting limit participation in elections. Voting gives Californians a voice in public policies that affect their lives and communities, including decisions about how public resources are raised and spent. The report highlights the historical connection between democratic participation and taxation and argues that policies that make it harder for people to vote can also limit the ability of communities — particularly young people, people with low incomes, and people of color — to have a say in decisions about public investments and taxes.
“When you make it harder to vote, you make it harder to have fair representation or a say in decisions that shape your community — like how tax dollars get raised and spent,” added Graves.
Who’s At Risk
The report shows that about 2.7 million voting-age Californians who are US citizens do not have a driver’s license , while more than 3 million have a driver’s license that is expired, from another state, or lacks updated information. Nearly one-quarter of voting-age Californians without a driver’s license also lack a California state ID card. The measure could disproportionately affect people of color, young people, people with lower incomes, and people with disabilities, who are less likely to have a driver’s license. Prop. 39 would also impose substantial costs on state and local governments, with the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimating annual costs could range from tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars. The measure provides no new revenue to pay for these expenses.
The analysis also finds that Prop. 39’s citizenship verification requirements could incorrectly flag eligible US citizens due to errors, inconsistencies, and outdated information in government databases. Voters whose citizenship is mistakenly called into question could face burdensome processes to correct their records and could potentially lose their ability to vote if they fail to resolve the issue before an election. More broadly, requiring identifying information on ballot envelopes could increase the risk of identity theft and potentially discourage Californians from using the state’s most common method of voting.
Rather than creating additional barriers to voting, the report identifies ways California can strengthen voter participation and improve the election process. These include exploring options for moving toward automatic voter registration, providing dedicated funding for voter outreach and engagement, supporting civic education, and investing in county election offices and systems that could help accelerate ballot counting while maintaining election security and voter access.
California voters will decide on Proposition 39 in November. The Budget Center’s analysis provides information on the measure’s proposed requirements, potential impacts, and fiscal implications to help Californians understand the choices before them.
To view the full publication and additional analyses, visit www.calbudgetcenter.org/resources/ (http://www.calbudgetcenter.org/resources/) .

Endorsement: Prop 39 would create CEQA for voting rights. No thanks
Even if you think voter fraud is a problem in California (it’s not), Prop 39 would turn our elections into a never-ending lawsuit
Proposition 39 would require Californians to present or incorporate some form of identification when voting. It is almost certain to disenfranchise eligible voters. The Chronicle’s editorial board recommends a no vote.
Todd Trumbull/S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 12, 2026
Is voter fraud rampant in California?
A May poll by the Public Policy Institute of California (https://data.ddhq.io/polls/2026/05/30/Public-Policy-Institute-of-California-California) found that 41% of likely voters here were either “very” or “somewhat” concerned that it’s too easy for ineligible voters to cast ballots.
That’s not an insignificant number.
Chronicle endorsements: Editorial Board’s recommendations for 2026 election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
So, how can California shore up trust?
Carl DeMaio, the firebrand Republican Assembly member from San Diego, claims to have the answer: Proposition 39 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
The measure would create a host of new voter-identification requirements in California and mandate regular election audits. Prop 39 was placed on the November ballot via a signature-gathering effort by volunteers from DeMaio’s advocacy organization (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/02/carl-demaio-california-maga-voter-id-prop-39-01103730?nname=california-playbook&nid=00000150-384f-da43-aff2-bf7fd35a0000&nrid=adfb3333-039f-4cee-9cbe-7aea15435a8e), Reform California, and paid operatives funded by Julie Luckey (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook-pm/2025/11/24/the-donor-powering-a-voter-id-push-in-california-00667090), whose son Palmer was recently named as a leader of the Trump administration’s new Project Meridian war council (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/pentagon-weapon-military-war-22464710.php).
Even though wealthy out-of-state Republicans have largely funded the yes campaign, DeMaio inexplicably insisted to the editorial board that the measure is “a balanced, bipartisan approach.”
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 39 is “the best way to shut down the conspiracy theories that irresponsible politicians spread,” DeMaio said.
Well, no.
The best way is for those irresponsible politicians, paramount among them DeMaio’s ally, President Donald Trump, to stop sowing unfounded disbelief.
Because by every available measure, California’s voting system is working.
The California State Library’s research bureau examined reports from 14 counties (https://www.library.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/crb-reports/CRB-Voter-Fraud-Presentation-Senate-Elections-2026-04-03.pdf) where grand juries investigated voter fraud risks from 2020 to 2024 and found an overwhelming consensus: no evidence of systemic or significant fraud. Even the right-wing Heritage Foundation — the organization behind Project 2025 — identified just 71 instances of known voter fraud in California (https://electionfraud.heritage.org/search?case_type=All&fraud_type=All&state=CA) from 1982 to 2025.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
All of those cases were prosecuted — evidence that California takes election integrity seriously. In fact, the state rejected its highest percentage of mail ballots in more than a decade (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-mail-ballot-rejections-22359196.php) for the June 2 primary — largely because they were postmarked after Election Day or arrived too late. There was also an uptick in signatures that election officials couldn’t verify.
Yet Prop 39 supporters insist on the need for additional identity verification.
To understand Prop 39’s proposed changes and the impact, let’s first look at the state’s existing processes:
Under California law (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration), anyone registering to vote must prove their identity via their driver’s license, state identification number or the last four digits of their Social Security number. Election officials check this identification against state and federal databases. Voters must also attest under penalty of perjury — which carries a potential prison sentence — that they’re a U.S. citizen living in California who’s at least 18 years old and not currently in prison or found incapable of voting by a court.
Every registered voter in California then receives a mail-in ballot, which most residents prefer (more than 80% voted this way in the past election). Before counting it, election officials check whether the voter’s signature on the outside of the ballot matches the signature on file (usually from a driver’s license). If it doesn’t, election officials give voters a chance to “cure” it by notifying them of the issue and providing a correction form (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2026-general/november-3-2026-general-combo-statement.pdf), which they have 22 days to return.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
People voting in person typically don’t have to present ID, but they do have to sign a registration list at the polls.
Prop 39 would change all that. To vote by mail, Californians would have to preselect a form of government-issued identification and write the last four digits of that ID on the outside of their ballot.
To vote in person, Californians would need to show a government-issued ID. Prop 39 mandates the state provide free “voter identification cards” — which do not currently exist — to those who request them. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop39-110326.pdf) estimated that creating these cards, in addition to other expenses resulting from Prop 39, could cost local and state governments hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
The measure also requires state and local elections officials to employ “best efforts” to verify registered voters are U.S. citizens and to publish annual reports revealing the percentage of verified voters. It mandates the state auditor to review compliance every other year.
What forms of government-issued ID would be acceptable under Prop 39, and how would voters preselect the ID they want to use for their 4-digit PIN? Do they get a chance to cure their ballots if they write the wrong digits on their vote-by-mail envelope? And what would be considered “best efforts” to verify someone’s citizenship status — given that even the federal government doesn’t have a comprehensive list of citizens?
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 39 directs the state Legislature to “promptly” enact laws to answer these questions. It also creates a private right of action that permits any person who believes state or local government isn’t complying with the measure to take those entities to court.
Justin Levitt, a constitutional and election law expert at the Loyola Law School, called this a “generic litigation trap” that opens the door to countless frivolous lawsuits.
Just as the California Environmental Quality Act enables aggrieved NIMBYs to weaponize the legal system against development projects they dislike, Prop 39 will do the same with elections.
“You will have plenty of advocacy organizations that are eager to sue over perceived noncompliance with this initiative early and often,” Levitt told the editorial board.
And Prop 39 is almost certain to disenfranchise eligible voters.
Large numbers of California U.S. citizens lack either IDs or proof of citizenship. A 2026 University of Maryland analysis (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/Who%20Lacks%20ID%20and%20Proof%20of%20Citizenship%20in%20California%20Today_.pdf) found that about 2.7 million Californians, or about 11% of eligible voters, don’t have a driver’s license, while 13% have one that’s expired or has an outdated address or name. People of color, young residents, disabled Californians and lower-income residents are disproportionately represented in these groups.
The study also found 24% of Californians don’t have a passport and that more than 3 million voting-age Californians would have difficulty readily accessing documents proving their citizenship.
In short, Prop 39 would do little to stop the minimal fraud that exists while creating millions “more chances for valid ballots to be rejected,” Abdi Soltani, executive director of ACLU of Northern California, told the editorial board.
After Texas passed a similar voter-ID law in 2021, its rate of rejected ballots skyrocketed from less than 1% to more than 12% (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/), effectively invalidating 1 in 8 votes cast in the 2022 primary. A peer-reviewed study (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/737439) found it also reduced voter turnout in subsequent elections.
About Opinion
The editorial positions of The Chronicle, including election recommendations, represent the consensus of the editorial board , consisting of the publisher, the editorial page editor and staff members of the opinion pages. Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
California could do more to assuage concerns about election integrity. Counties have been begging the state for permission to join a nonprofit, multistate organization that helps officials improve the accuracy of their voter rolls (https://apcp.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2024-04/ab-2050-pellerin-apcp-analysis_1.pdf).
But Prop 39 is a nakedly bad-faith effort designed to encourage frivolous lawsuits, deepen distrust, increase political polarization and waste taxpayer dollars. Vote no.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)

It’s impossible not to view Proposition 39 — the measure authored by Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio and backed by out-of-state, right-wing billionaires (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-election-voter-id-proposition-39/) — strictly through the lens of national politics.
In requiring voters to show IDs before receiving their ballots (among other restrictive voting rules and audits), it gives credence to President Donald Trump’s longstanding and repeatedly debunked claims that millions of noncitizens routinely vote in U.S. elections.

Endorsement: Break the 49ers' grip over Santa Clara. Elect these three candidates. (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/31/endorsement-break-the-49ers-grip-over-santa-clara-make-kertes-mayor-elect-inciarte-and-crutchlow-to-council/)

Endorsement: Elect Michael Melillo to San Jose Unified School District Board of Education (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-michael-melillo-to-san-jose-unified-school-district-board-of-education/)
Endorsement: Reject San Mateo Community College District’s $848 million Measure V (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-reject-san-mateo-community-college-districts-848-million-measure-v/)
Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
This initiative is an expensive solution to a phantom problem. Reject Prop. 39.
Manufactured crisis
Multiple groups have studied the issue and found scant evidence of widespread fraud. The California State Library (https://www.library.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/crb-reports/CRB-Voter-Fraud-Presentation-Senate-Elections-2026-04-03.pdf) looked at 14 counties where grand juries issued reports on the risk of voter fraud in the 2020, 2022 and 2024 elections and found secure elections everywhere. The Brennan Center for Justice’s research confirmed that voter fraud is a myth (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/debunking-voter-fraud-myth). Even the conservative Heritage Foundation could only find 71 instances (https://electionfraud.heritage.org/search?case_type=All&fraud_type=All&state=CA) of voter fraud in California — over more than four decades. Also, California already takes election integrity (https://abc7news.com/post/150000-mail-ballots-rejected-californias-primary-despite-efforts-count-every-vote/19571066/) seriously, which is one reason our process of confirming elections is so slow (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/17/upshot/california-slow-election-results.html).
RELATED: Endorsement Cheat Sheet: Mercury News and East Bay Times Editorial Boards’ top picks for California’s Nov. 3 general election (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/13/bay-area-news-group-california-election-endorsements-november-2026/)
Our editorial board repeatedly asked the Yes on Prop. 39 campaign for evidence of voter fraud in California, rampant or otherwise, and they deflected, dodged and denied the premise of our questions. They insisted that fraud wasn’t actually the issue — that Prop. 39 is about improving public trust and confidence in our democracy.
So it’s purely coincidence that Donald Trump demanded “voter ID” laws in California as a condition for wildfire disaster relief (https://abc7.com/post/president-donald-trump-wants-voter-id-laws-condition-aid-california/15833908/) last year. Or that the measure’s biggest backer, Illinois billionaire Richard Uihlein, has a history ofcontributing (https://www.propublica.org/article/uline-uihlein-election-denial) to the campaigns of election deniers.
According to the Public Policy Institute of California (https://data.ddhq.io/polls/2026/05/30/Public-Policy-Institute-of-California-California), a quarter of likely voters are very concerned that it’s too easy for ineligible people to vote. That’s not zero, but it also doesn’t mean we should be changing election laws to accommodate the fact-free fears of a minority of Californians.
In other polls about trust in our elections, it is overwhelmingly Republicans who are the most concerned. That’s fine. But if they really cared about improving those numbers, we’d recommend they start by asking the president to stop spreading false information.
We absolutely wouldn’t recommend, as Prop. 39 does, that private citizens be allowed to sue if they believe the government isn’t complying with the measure’s rules. We don’t even want to imagine the kind of frivolous litigation that could inspire.
Why panic?
It’s possible to view Prop. 39 and say, “What’s the big deal?” Thirty-six statesrequire (https://ballotpedia.org/Voter_identification_laws_by_state) voters to present identification before voting in person.
Well, the big deal is that a lot of eligible people might not be able to vote if the measure is passed. Millions of Californians (https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/Who%20Lacks%20ID%20and%20Proof%20of%20Citizenship%20in%20California%20Today_.pdf) wouldn’t have the ID required to satisfy this proposal. (They’d have to request a new one.) And, as the No on Prop. 39 campaign pointed out to us, when Texas implemented similar mail-ballot ID rules, rejections shot up (https://www.texastribune.org/2022/04/06/texas-mail-in-ballot-rejection-voting/) from 1% to 12%.
Plus, completely revamping the voter verification system will come with financial costs — “between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year,” according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Prop. 39 isn’t just about voter ID. It contains a provision that is deeply problematic: requiring election officials to use their “best efforts” to verify the citizenship status of voters they register, with regular audits to ensure compliance.
But there is no reliable government list of U.S. citizens. The Supreme Court decided that the federal government could continue to try to create one, but it’s already full of mistakes (https://www.npr.org/2026/09/25/nx-s1-5976804/supreme-court-trump-save-noncitizen-voting), labeling many citizens as ineligible to vote.
This deeply flawed measure would create chaos for no reason.
Reject Prop. 39.

I am reviewing academic literature on voter ID turnout effects and the University of Maryland study. I am also weighing any strong arguments for voting yes.

The evidence points to a "no" vote. Documented voter fraud in California is extremely rare, with only 71 instances found over roughly 40 years and noncitizen voting at vanishingly low rates.

The measure would cost tens to hundreds of millions of dollars annually with no dedicated revenue source. Its design is also flawed: it requires the last four digits of a specific government ID on mail-in ballots, and Texas's similar rule rejected over 24,000 ballots in one primary.

Texas's similar rule also reduced turnout and created racial disparities in rejections. The constitutional text lacks a cure process for rejected ballots, unlike signature matching.

The measure would create a litigation trap. Vague "best efforts" citizenship verification combined with annual public reporting of unverified percentages and private right of action invites lawsuits. No reliable comprehensive database exists, and existing systems like SAVE produce false positives that wrongly flag citizens. Because the requirements are constitutional, they are difficult to fix.

Free voter ID is not automatic and still requires bureaucratic navigation. Millions of Californians lack valid IDs, so obtaining documents to prove identity carries real costs. Exposing partial ID numbers on mail ballots also increases identity theft risk because those ballots travel through the postal system.

The current system already verifies identity through existing databases, signature matching with a cure process, and citizenship attestation under penalty of perjury. The claimed benefits are weak, and evidence on whether the measure increases public trust is mixed.

The yes campaign frames the measure as a trust issue rather than a documented fraud problem. The claim that voter ID laws increase participation is not causally supported; turnout trends are driven by many factors, and Texas's similar rule actually reduced participation.

Academic and GAO research on strict photo ID laws shows small to moderate negative turnout effects, concentrated among minorities, young, elderly, and low-income voters. Even null effects do not justify rejecting valid ballots or spending hundreds of millions of dollars when the prevented fraud is near zero. Signature matching already rejects over 100,000 ballots annually, so adding numeric matching does not clearly improve accuracy.

The measure is heavily funded by out-of-state conservative donors and led by Carl DeMaio. Major California editorial boards and civil rights organizations oppose it. A few local news groups support it. Recent polls show most likely voters oppose the measure after hearing arguments.

A few arguments for yes remain. Requiring ID is a standard principle in most life transactions, and thirty-six states already have some form of voter ID. Supporters also note that signature matching is flawed, with over one hundred thousand ballots rejected and two hundred thousand causing hassles. A numeric ID could be simpler for voters who do not remember their signature style.

Prop 39 does not replace signature verification. It adds numeric ID matching on top of existing checks, so voters could face both requirements. Forty-one percent of likely California voters worry that ineligible people can vote too easily, and public confidence in the integrity of elections is central to democratic legitimacy.

This measure is neither low-cost nor well-designed. Automatic and DMV registration creates theoretical vulnerabilities where noncitizens might be registered by mistake, though audits show most noncitizens on rolls are administrative errors or people who later became citizens. "Best efforts" verification could catch such data errors.

Database matching carries high false-positive rates relative to true positives when the base rate of ineligible registration is tiny. Kansas and Georgia have wrongly flagged citizens. The measure provides no safeguards against erroneous removal.

Biennial State Auditor reviews are a reasonable good-government idea that could be passed separately without the rest of the measure.

The measure is self-executing, so the ID requirement would bind before the free voter ID system is built. That creates a serious transition risk where the constitutional mandate could be enforced while the infrastructure does not yet exist.

Texas SB1 is the relevant precedent, not Georgia photo ID, because Prop 39 targets mail-ballot ID-number matching in a universal vote-by-mail state. I am now checking whether the measure repeals signature requirements and whether a cure process is implied.

The text confirms the measure does not replace signature verification. It mandates a last-four-digit ID number on mail ballots and requires identity verification before counting any regular or provisional ballot.

The constitutional text does not require a cure process for rejected ballots. The legislature must pass implementing laws, but a hostile or slow legislature could leave the requirement unenforced. Even a friendly legislature's cure process could be challenged by citizens under the private right of action if it undermines the verification requirement. The definition of "government-issued identification" is also vague and could be litigated to exclude various valid IDs.

The citizenship verification requirement does not explicitly mandate purging unverified voters, yet public reporting of county-level percentages and the threat of private lawsuits create strong pressure to remove them. Matching citizens to citizenship databases is inherently error-prone due to naturalization status, name changes, and data entry mistakes. The evidence points to a clear "no" vote.

# Strict ID Laws Don’t Stop Voters: Evidence from a U.S. Nationwide Panel, 2008–2018
Using a difference-in-differences design on a 1.6-billion-observations panel dataset, 2008–2018, we find that the laws have no negative effect on registration or turnout, overall or for any group defined by race, gender, age, or party affiliation.
...
Based on this specification, we obtain point estimates of -0.1 percentage point for effects both on overall registration and turnout (with 95 percent confidence intervals of [-2.3; 2.1pp] and [-3.0; 2.8pp], respectively), and +1.4pp for the effect on the turnout of non-white voters relative to whites (with a 95 percent confidence interval of [-0.5; 3.2pp]).
The lack of negative impact on voter turnout cannot be attributed to voters’ reaction against the laws, measured by campaign contributions and self-reported political engagement.

Issue Brief
Proposition 39 Explained: What Voter ID Would Mean for California
A Look at How Proposed Identification Requirements Would Impact Millions of California Voters
September 2026 | By Scott Graves (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/scott-graves/), Alissa Anderson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/alissa-anderson/), and Leslie A. Ortiz (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/leslie-a-ortiz/)
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 39 on the November ballot would impose unnecessary, harmful, and costly new identification (ID) requirements on millions of California voters. It would harm US citizens by making it harder for them to vote, exposing them to identity theft, and putting them at risk of being erroneously removed from voter rolls. Prop. 39 is part of broader national efforts to create new barriers to voting, which primarily impact people with low incomes, young people, and people of color, limiting Californians’ say in how public tax dollars are raised and spent.
Table Of Contents
What Would Prop. 39 Do?
How Would Prop. 39 Affect Californians and the State?
Prop. 39 Is Part of a Nationwide Effort to Restrict Voting and Limit People’s Say in Policymaking
California Should Continue to Promote Voter Participation and Improve the Election Process
Prop. 39 Supporters and Opponents
What Would Prop. 39 Do?
Prop. 39 would amend California’s Constitution to add new voter ID requirements that would affect current and future voters. The measure would also impose new responsibilities on state and local officials related to election administration. Specifically, Prop. 39:
Requires Elections Officials to “Use Best Efforts” to Verify Every Registered Voter’s Citizenship Status
Current Law
Californians are required (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voting-resources/voting-california/who-can-vote-california) to be US citizens to vote. 1 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 2101(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=2101.). There are two exceptions: Oakland and San Francisco allow certain noncitizens to vote in local school board elections. To register to vote, a person must declare in writing, under penalty of perjury, that they meet all voter eligibility requirements, including that they are a US citizen (https://covr.sos.ca.gov/). 2 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 2150(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=2150.). Under federal law (https://www.justice.gov/crt/national-voter-registration-act-1993-nvra), state motor vehicle agencies — like California’s Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) — must provide residents with the opportunity to register to vote when they apply for or renew a driver’s license or state ID card and/or change their address. In California, this is known as Motor Voter (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/california-motor-voter/frequently-asked-questions). DMV customers who indicate that they are eligible to vote are registered to vote by the Secretary of State (SOS) unless they opt out. However, the DMV does not send to the SOS (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/california-motor-voter/frequently-asked-questions) information regarding customers who indicate they are not eligible to vote. Falsely claiming to be a US citizen on a voter registration application and attempting to vote would expose a person to state felony charges as well as the possibility of deportation under federal law. 3 (javascript:void(0)) For example, see California Elections Code, Section 18560(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18560.), 8 U.S.C. Section 1227(a)(6)(a) (https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title8-section1227&num=0&edition=prelim), and 18 U.S.C. Section 611 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/611).
In addition, state law makes it a crime to:
Vote or attempt to vote more than once in an election,
Impersonate or attempt to impersonate a voter in an election, or
Apply for or cast a vote-by-mail ballot by fraudulently signing the name of a fake person, another qualified voter, or a person who is not qualified to vote. 4 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 18560(b)-(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18560.) and Section 18578 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=18578.).
A person who is convicted of any of these crimes could be imprisoned for up to three years.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require state and county election officials to “use best efforts” to verify, using “government data,” that registered voters are US citizens. The measure does not define “best efforts” or what constitutes “government data.” In addition, election officials would have to annually report the share of registered voters in each county whose citizenship status has been verified.
Requires Voters to Present Additional Identifying Information When They Cast Their Ballot
Current Law
All states, including California, already have voter ID requirements (https://electionlab.mit.edu/research/voter-identification) as required by federal law (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/hava-id-standards). For example, to register to vote, Californians must provide (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) a California driver’s license or state ID number or the last four digits of their Social Security Number (SSN) if they lack a driver’s license or ID card. Californians who lack a driver’s license, a state ID card, or a SSN are assigned a unique identifier (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) to validate their registration. Californians generally are not required (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) to present an ID when voting. 5 (javascript:void(0)) Californians may need to show (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/voter-registration) an acceptable form of ID when they vote by mail or in person if all of the following apply: 1) they’re voting for the first time in a federal election, 2) they registered by mail or online, and 3) they did not provide a California ID or SSN when registering. Acceptable forms of ID (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/hava-id-standards) include, but aren’t limited to, a California driver’s license or state ID card, a US passport, a student or military ID, a utility bill, and a bank statement.
When voting by mail, California voters sign the outside of their ballot envelope, and elections officials verify the signature before counting the ballot. 6 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 3011(a)(7) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3011.) and Section 3019 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3019.). Voters must be given an opportunity to correct or “cure” their ballot if they failed to sign the envelope or if their signature does not match the signature on file. 7 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Sections 3019(c)-(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=3019.).
When voting in person, California voters state their name and address and sign a list of registered voters under penalty of perjury. 8 (javascript:void(0)) California Elections Code, Section 14216(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=ELEC&sectionNum=14216.). While election officials do not verify (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm) the signatures of in-person voters before counting their ballots, counties have procedures in place to prevent voter fraud. 9 (javascript:void(0)) For example, in many counties, poll workers are able to look up voting records in real time to ensure that a voter has not already cast a ballot in the election. This applies to counties that participate (https://www.sos.ca.gov/voters-choice-act/vca-participating-counties) in California’s Voter’s Choice Act (https://www.sos.ca.gov/voters-choice-act) as well as to counties that have adopted the Sign, Scan, and Go (https://www.placercountyelections.gov/sign-scan-go/) option. As noted above, it is a crime in California to fraudulently vote in an election, to vote more than once, or to impersonate another voter. Penalties range from up to one year in a county jail to up to three years in state prison.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would impose new requirements on Californians to cast a ballot in person or mail a ballot.
To vote in person:
Voters would have to present a “government-issued” ID when they arrive at their polling place. Prop. 39 does not specifically define what “government-issued” ID means, so the Legislature would need to clarify which types of ID a voter could present to prove their identity. 10 (javascript:void(0)) Prop. 39 says broadly that “government-issued” ID “means documentation that allows conclusive verification of the voter’s identity.”
To vote by mail:
All new and existing voters would have to select a “government-issued” ID that would be reflected in their “voter registration record.” This requirement effectively means that people who are currently registered to vote would have to re-register to provide their chosen ID to election officials.
When voting, voters would have to write on the outside of their ballot envelope the last four digits of a “unique identifying number” from the “government-issued” ID that they selected for the purpose of voting. 11 (javascript:void(0)) The government-issued ID that voters choose for this purpose would have to subsequently be made available to them “on request by phone or electronically.”
Election officials would verify that the four digits written on the envelope match the last four digits of the ID number in the voter’s registration record.
Requires the State to Create a New Voter ID Card
Current Law
California currently allows Californians to apply for three types of ID cards (https://www.dmv.ca.gov/portal/driver-licenses-identification-cards/identification-id-cards/) in addition to drivers’ licenses that are used to prove identity or age. 12 (javascript:void(0)) The ID cards are issued by the California Department of Motor Vehicles as alternatives to a driver’s license and cannot be used to operate a motor vehicle.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the state to provide a voter ID card to eligible voters who request one. Voters could use this optional ID as their “government-issued” ID for voting by mail or in person. This card would be provided to voters free of charge.
Requires Ongoing State Audits of How the State and Counties Are Complying with Prop. 39
Current Law
California’s independently elected (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/california-state-constitutional-offices-defined/) Secretary of State oversees (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/about-agency) all elections in the state, including ensuring election laws are enforced, testing and approving voting equipment, compiling election returns, and certifying election results.
In addition, California’s independent, nonpartisan State Auditor (https://www.auditor.ca.gov/about-us/) conducts performance audits and investigations of various state and local government agencies and recommends solutions for improving services. However, the State Auditor currently does not have a formal, ongoing role in auditing California’s elections or evaluating election administration.
Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the State Auditor, in odd-numbered years, to audit state and county compliance with Prop. 39 and report any recommendations for improvement.
Requires the State Legislature to Pass Laws to Implement Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would require the Legislature to “promptly enact laws” to implement the measure. For example, legislators would have to define which kinds of “government-issued” ID would be acceptable for voting as well as clarify what it means to make a “best effort” to verify a voter’s citizenship status. Prop. 39 would also require the Legislature to establish rules for military and overseas voters that are consistent with federal law.
Allows Citizens to Sue the State or Any County for Not Complying with Prop. 39
Prop. 39 would allow private citizens to sue the state and/or any county for any alleged noncompliance with the initiative. The measure does not specify what kind of evidence would be required to file a lawsuit.
How Would Prop. 39 Affect Californians and the State?
Prop. 39 Would Waste Resources By Addressing a Nonexistent Problem
The voter ID requirements that Prop. 39 would establish provide a “solution” to a nonexistent problem. This measure is based on the false premise that voter fraud — casting a ballot when one is not eligible to vote — is undermining election integrity. However, research shows that voter fraud is exceedingly rare. For example:
Using a comprehensive database tracking election fraud (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/how-widespread-is-election-fraud-in-the-united-states-not-very/) that was created by the right-wing think tank Heritage Foundation, the Brookings Institute found across more than 200 federal elections held in recent decades, the share of fraudulent votes cast were infinitesimally small — ranging from roughly 3 to 15 votes out of 10 million in seven states with close election outcomes. The study concluded that “isolated instances of fraud do not constitute a widespread trend” and that “no election outcome in the US has ever been altered by ballot fraud.”
Summarizing findings across numerous academic studies and investigative reports, the Brennan Center for Justice (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/debunking-voter-fraud-myth) concludes that cases of voter impersonation fraud are extremely rare and do not happen “on a scale even close to that necessary to ‘rig’ an election.” For instance, their seminal report, The Truth About Voter Fraud (https://www.brennancenter.org/media/179/download/Report_Truth-About-Voter-Fraud.pdf?inline=1), concluded that “it is more likely that an individual will be struck by lightning than that [they] will impersonate another voter at the polls.”
Voter fraud among noncitizens is also extremely rare. The Brennan Center (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/noncitizen-voting-vanishingly-rare) synthesized findings from comprehensive studies, state investigations, and nationwide surveys across more than two decades and concluded that “actual incidents of noncitizens voting is not a significant occurrence.” For instance:
One national survey (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/noncitizen-voting-missing-millions) of 44 election administrators representing 42 jurisdictions in 12 states, including officials in eight of the 10 jurisdictions with the largest populations of noncitizens nationally, found that in the 2016 election, officials referred only about 30 incidents of suspected noncitizen voting for further investigation or prosecution — amounting to 0.0001% of votes cast.
The Bipartisan Policy Institute (https://bipartisanpolicy.org/article/four-things-to-know-about-noncitizen-voting/) concluded that “there is no evidence that noncitizen voting has ever been significant enough to impact an election’s outcome.” Allegations of noncitizens voting often come out of voter registration audits, but further investigation into these claims often shows that individuals were flagged as noncitizens erroneously.
The libertarian think tank Cato Institute (https://www.cato.org/blog/noncitizens-dont-illegally-vote-detectable-numbers) found that “there is no good evidence that noncitizens voted illegally [in the 2020 election] in large enough numbers to actually shift the outcome of elections or even change the number of electoral votes.”
Additionally, while proponents of Prop. 39 argue that imposing additional ID requirements will strengthen voters’ trust in California’s election process, evidence for this claim is lacking. One study (https://review.law.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2016/08/6_-_Persily_-_Stan._L._Rev.pdf) found that registered voters had roughly equal confidence that votes were counted accurately whether they were in states with strict voter ID laws or states with the minimum ID requirements mandated by federal law.
Subsequent studies by researchers at the University of California Riverside and Western Washington University looking at voter perceptions in 2014 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/1532440015624102?) and following the 2020 US presidential election (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10659129231206179) found that strict voter ID laws and the quality of election administration more generally had little to no effect on voter confidence. This and other research (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10659129241283169) suggests this may be because voters view election laws through a partisan lens and their confidence may be more heavily influenced by partisan rhetoric and whether their preferred candidate wins or loses an election. 13 (javascript:void(0)) See Lonna Rae Atkeson, Eli McKown-Dawson, and Robert M.
